source.title_on_document: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary

supplement.where: Supplementary Figures S1-S7 in this PDF (pp. 11-16). Data and code are listed at https://github.com/berenslab/llm-excess-vocab (p. 8, Section 4.7).
supplement.holds: Excess-word plots for 2013-2023 (Figures S1-S4, pp. 11-14), unique-lemma counts (S5, p. 15), the list of 291 rare excess style words (S6, p. 15), and the t-SNE map of local Delta for 4,109,080 abstracts from 2022-2024 (S7, p. 16). Figure S7 explains the local comparison of marker-word fractions among 100 neighboring abstracts from 2022 and 100 from 2024. No standard errors or confidence intervals for the LLM-usage estimates are reported in the main text or supplementary figures. Section 4.7 states that the GitHub repository provides the yearly word-occurrence matrix and content/style annotations.

paper_design_summary: The authors analyzed 15,103,888 English-language PubMed abstracts from 2010-2024 and counted yearly word-occurrence frequencies (p. 7, Sections 4.1-4.3). They compared observed 2024 frequencies with counterfactual extrapolations from 2021 and 2022, using two sets of excess style words to estimate a lower bound on LLM-assisted writing, overall and by field, country, journal, and inferred author gender (pp. 4-5, Sections 2.2-2.3). No people were assigned to AI assistance, and the measured outcome is LLM-use prevalence rather than creativity or diversity (p. 5, Discussion; p. 7, Methods).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing. The study compares word frequencies in published abstracts across years: observed 2024 frequencies against a counterfactual extrapolated from 2021-2022.
assignment.quote: we study vocabulary changes in over 15 million biomedical abstracts from 2010–2024 indexed by PubMed, and show how the appearance of LLMs led to an abrupt increase in the frequency of certain style words.

participants.exclusions: Corpus filters, not participant exclusions: 24,814,136 complete English-language abstracts of 250-4000 characters were identified; 15,103,888 abstracts from publication years 2010-2024 were analyzed. Cleaning affected 286,744 abstracts, and 3,514 abstracts of errata, corrigenda, correction, or retraction notices were entirely erased. The paper still reports 15,103,888 rows in the resulting word-occurrence matrix (p. 7, Sections 4.1-4.2); no additional subtraction from that reported analysis count is made.
participants.who: No human participants. The corpus is abstracts written by the authors of PubMed-indexed biomedical papers (scientists). The population code describes those authors and is nominal.
participants.country: Multiple: worldwide PubMed corpus. Country is the first affiliation of the first author; the 50 countries with the most papers are analyzed separately.
participants.quote: This resulted in 24 814 136 abstracts. We then only analyzed papers with publication years from 2010 to 2024, giving us 15 103 888 abstracts for analysis.

ai_tool.name_model: Not specified; LLMs such as ChatGPT in general (use inferred from vocabulary, not observed)
ai_tool.how_used: Not observed. The paper infers at the corpus level that some 2024 abstracts were written or edited with LLMs, from excess style-word frequencies. It cannot identify individual abstracts (p. 5, Discussion).

task.description: Writing abstracts of biomedical papers (real publications indexed by PubMed). Not a creative or ideation task as the codebook defines it.

outcomes.name: Frequency gap of excess style marker words (lower bound on the share of 2024 abstracts processed with LLMs)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Delta_G = P_G - Q_G: the observed minus the counterfactual expected fraction of 2024 abstracts containing at least one word from marker set G (p. 4). Word frequencies are p = (a+1)/(b+1), and the counterfactual is q = p_-2 + 2*max{p_-2 - p_-3, 0}, a linear extrapolation from 2021 and 2022 (p. 7, Section 4.3). Two non-overlapping sets: 291 rare excess style words with 2024 frequency below T = 0.02 (Figure S6) and 10 common ones (across, additionally, comprehensive, crucial, enhancing, exhibited, insights, notably, particularly, within). The final estimate averages the two gaps. Variants treated as the same outcome: single-word gaps (potential, delta = 0.052; pp. 2-3) and subgroup Delta estimates by field, country, journal, and inferred gender (pp. 4-5). The local t-SNE variant instead subtracts marker-word fractions among 100 neighboring 2022 abstracts from those among 100 neighboring 2024 abstracts, then averages the rare- and common-word gaps (p. 16, Figure S7). It measures how much LLM-processed text exists, not creativity or diversity. lexical_overlap is the nearest measure code: the score is a word-occurrence frequency, not an overlap between outputs. ai_available is 'mixed' for the cross-year corpus comparison: the paper dates ChatGPT's release to November 2022 (p. 1), uses 2021-2022 as the baseline, and excludes 2023 from the counterfactual because it could already reflect LLM use (p. 2); no author's actual use or access is observed. n_units is the 15,103,888 abstracts (2010-2024) analyzed in the full matrix (p. 7), not a people count or a count specific to the 2024 contrast. The 2024 Delta draws on the 2021, 2022, and 2024 abstracts, whose yearly counts the paper does not print (over 1 million per year, p. 2).

contrasts.treatment_arm: 2024 abstracts: observed fraction containing at least one marker word (P)
contrasts.control_arm: Counterfactual expected 2024 fraction (Q), linearly extrapolated from 2021 and 2022
contrasts.reported: Delta_rare = 0.136 (291 rare style words, T = 0.02); Delta_common = 0.134 (10 common style words); Delta = (Delta_common + Delta_rare)/2 = 0.135, 'at least 13.5%' of 2024 abstracts. Covid comparison (covid, pandemic, coronavirus, sars; 2021): Delta = 0.069. Subgroups in the text: computation and bioinformatics about 0.20; United Kingdom and Australia about 0.05; China, South Korea, Taiwan about 0.20; inferred gender 0.09 male, 0.07-0.08 female; Sensors 0.25; Cureus 0.20; MDPI 0.21; Frontiers 0.20; Nature+Science+Cell 0.07; Nature family 0.10; South Korea x Sensors 0.34; China x computation 0.41; local t-SNE areas about 0.50. Figure 5e labels: computation 0.24, environment 0.20, bioinformatics 0.21, UK 0.04, China 0.20, Cureus 0.20, Sensors 0.25, Frontiers 0.20, MDPI 0.21, Nature family 0.10, China comp. 0.41, Korea Sensors 0.34. Range across subcorpora: below 5% to over 40%. Point estimates only: no standard errors, intervals, tests, or p-values. Observed and expected levels appear only in Figures 4a and 5a.

data_and_code.data_url: https://github.com/berenslab/llm-excess-vocab (yearly word-occurrence matrix as csv.gz, content/style annotations as csv); raw PubMed data at https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/download

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is not met: this is an observational corpus analysis, with no assignment of people to AI assistance; LLM use is inferred at corpus level and cannot be identified for individual abstracts (p. 5, Discussion; p. 7, Sections 4.1-4.3). Criterion 2 is not met: the 15,103,888 observations analyzed are PubMed abstracts, not participants, and the paper reports no participant cohort or people count (p. 7, Sections 4.1-4.2); the people counts remain null. Criterion 3 is not met: excess marker-word frequencies are computed on abstract text, but estimate the prevalence of LLM-assisted writing, not creativity, novelty, or diversity across authors (pp. 3-4, Section 2.2). Homogenisation is discussed with citations to other studies (p. 6, Discussion), and the t-SNE supplement maps local LLM-use estimates rather than measuring an AI effect on diversity (p. 16, Figure S7). Codebook Section 3 excludes AI-text-prevalence studies without a diversity outcome from both the core dataset and observational context. The outstanding journal-version check concerns provenance and does not change these eligibility findings for the saved PDF.

one_line_finding: Excess style-word frequencies in 15.1 million analyzed PubMed abstracts (2010-2024; p. 7, Section 4.1) imply that at least 13.5 percent of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs (Delta = 0.135, the average of 0.136 for 291 rare words and 0.134 for 10 common words; p. 4, Section 2.2, Figure 5a), compared with a gap of 0.069 for 2021 Covid words (p. 4), and the lower bound ranges from below 5 percent to over 40 percent across subcorpora (p. 5, Discussion).

notes: No people, no assignment, no creativity or diversity measure. S1-O1 is recorded with question 'none' for documentation only (screener B listed no outcomes; see reconciliation). Other printed corpus-level numbers: 26.7 K words with p > 10^-4 in both 2023 and 2024 (p. 2); 454 excess words in 2024 versus up to 190 in 2021, and 343 versus 180 unique lemmas (p. 3, Figures 3 and S5); 900 unique excess words in 2013-2024, 51.3 percent content and 45.2 percent style words (p. 3); 379 excess style words in 2024, 66 percent verbs and 14 percent adjectives (p. 3, Figure 3b); about 1.5 million papers indexed per year, so at least 200,000 LLM-assisted papers per year (p. 5); 4,109,080 abstracts from 2022-2024 in the Figure S7 embedding (p. 16). The abstracts are parsed and filtered as in the authors' prior PubMed paper, González-Márquez et al. (2024), 'The landscape of biomedical research' (p. 7, Section 4.1). The authors state that they used no LLMs to write or edit the manuscript (p. 7, Section 4.6). The markdown matches the PDF (v5). Its figure text is scrambled, so every number here was checked on the PDF pages.
